title: Maintaining Muscular Function
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Musculoskeletal Injuries

headings.title: Introduction to Musculoskeletal Health
headings.content: The musculoskeletal system is an integrated framework that provides structural support, enables movement, and protects vital organs. Maintaining optimal muscular function depends on a continuous cycle of muscle protein synthesis, adequate neural stimulation, and regular physical activity. When muscles remain active, they maintain their cross-sectional area, contractile strength, and metabolic flexibility. Conversely, physical inactivity triggers a swift deconditioning process, leading to a decline in functional capacity and muscle mass. Nurses play a crucial role in safeguarding this system by recognizing early signs of decline and promoting timely interventions that keep patients moving.

headings.title: Pathophysiology of Muscle Atrophy and Immobility
headings.content: Muscle atrophy is the reduction in muscle mass and function resulting from disuse, denervation, or systemic disease. When a patient is bedridden or experiences prolonged immobilization, muscle protein breakdown outpaces protein synthesis. This imbalance leads to a visible shrinking of muscle fibers, particularly in the weight-bearing lower extremities and postural muscles. Beyond mass loss, prolonged immobility alters muscle fiber composition, shifting from fatigue-resistant slow-twitch fibers to fast-twitch fibers that fatigue rapidly. Joint contractures can also develop as shortened connective tissues, tendons, and ligaments tighten around inactive joints, permanently limiting flexibility.

headings.title: Assessment of Muscle Strength and Tone
headings.content: Evaluating the musculoskeletal system requires a systematic physical assessment encompassing muscle strength, tone, and joint mobility. Nurses use standardized grading scales, such as the Medical Research Council scale, to grade muscle strength from zero (no movement) to five (normal strength against full resistance). Muscle tone is assessed by feeling the muscle resistance during passive stretching; abnormalities can manifest as hypotonia (flaccidity) or hypertonia (spasticity). Joint mobility checks reveal any early restrictions before permanent contractures form. Regular documentation of these parameters establishes a baseline and highlights the effectiveness of nursing interventions.

headings.title: Range of Motion (ROM) Exercises
headings.content:
- **Passive ROM**: The nurse or caregiver moves the joint through its full range without any effort from the patient, preserving joint flexibility but not building muscle strength.
- **Active-Assistive ROM**: The patient uses their own muscle power with gentle guidance and support from the nurse to complete the movement.
- **Active ROM**: The patient independently moves each joint through its complete range of motion using their own muscular strength.

Performing these exercises consistently prevents stiffness, maintains joint lubrication, and prevents the formation of painful contractures.

headings.title: Nutritional Support for Muscle Maintenance
headings.content: Muscle tissue relies heavily on proper nutrition to repair daily micro-damage and sustain mass. Protein intake is especially critical because it supplies the essential amino acids needed for muscle protein synthesis. Patients who are bedridden or recovering from surgery often require higher protein levels to counteract the catabolic state triggered by illness. In addition to protein, adequate hydration, calcium, vitamin D, and sufficient overall caloric intake are necessary to support normal muscle contraction and bone health. Clinical collaboration with dietitians ensures that individualized nutritional care plans meet these heightened metabolic demands.

headings.title: Preventing Complications of Immobility
headings.content: Immobility affects far more than just the muscular system; it places the entire body at risk of cascading complications. Pressure injuries can develop over bony prominences due to unrelieved pressure and compromised skin perfusion. Venous stasis in the lower extremities significantly increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis, which can lead to life-threatening pulmonary embolisms. Lungs can also suffer as shallow breathing leads to atelectasis and retained secretions, increasing pneumonia risks. Nurses prevent these multi-system complications through scheduled position changes, early ambulation protocols, deep breathing exercises, and the use of specialized support surfaces.
